source_batch.unit_label: BFM Module C unit 3 (courseware unit 21): international equity and debt products

facts.statement: Regulatory environment for foreign investment (courseware): foreign investment in India is regulated under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA) and the regulations on transfer or issue of a security by a person resident outside India (2017). Foreign direct investment (FDI) is investment through capital instruments by a person resident outside India in an unlisted Indian company, or in 10 per cent or more of the post-issue paid-up equity capital of a listed Indian company on a fully diluted basis (the total shares that would be outstanding if all possible sources of conversion were exercised). If an existing FDI falls below 10 per cent, it continues to be treated as FDI. Foreign portfolio investment (FPI) is investment in capital instruments of a listed company below 10 per cent of post-issue paid-up equity on a fully diluted basis (and below 10 per cent of each series of debentures or preference shares). A foreign portfolio investor is a person registered under the securities regulator foreign portfolio investor regulations. Foreign investment is any investment by a person resident outside India on a repatriable basis in capital instruments of an Indian company or the capital of an LLP.

Prohibited sectors (courseware, concept only): foreign investment is prohibited in specified sectors such as lottery, gambling and betting, chit funds (except non-repatriation investment by non-resident Indians and overseas citizens), nidhi companies, trading in transferable development rights, real estate business and construction of farmhouses, manufacturing of cigars and tobacco products, and activities not open to private sector investment (atomic energy, railway operations); foreign technology collaboration for lottery, gambling and betting is also prohibited. A citizen or entity of certain neighbouring countries needs prior government approval to invest. The list is as stated in the courseware at its date and is not taught in detail.

Global Depository Receipts (courseware): a GDR is a negotiable receipt issued by a depository abroad and traded in overseas markets that entitles the holder to convert into a specified number of equity shares of an Indian company; the underlying shares are issued by the Indian company and held by an Indian custodian on behalf of the overseas depository. GDRs are denominated in foreign currency; the exchange risk is borne by the overseas investor; the number of equity shares per GDR is fixed under pricing norms. On issue, the equity of the company increases but its debt-equity ratio is not adversely affected; dividends are paid in rupees to the depository; the depository is entitled to vote the shares as it holds the equity on behalf of GDR holders. Limited two-way fungibility exists: a registered stock broker can buy shares in the market for conversion into ADRs/GDRs, and reissuance is permitted to the extent redeemed, so the total outstanding under the GDR issuance stays at the level originally approved. American Depository Receipts (ADRs) are traded in the United States, and soliciting investors for ADRs can be done only from the United States with disclosure under US accounting standards.

Indian Depository Receipts (courseware): companies incorporated outside India may issue Indian Depository Receipts (IDRs) through a domestic depository to persons resident in India and persons resident outside India, in compliance with the company law rules for foreign companies and the securities regulator issue and disclosure requirements; issues by financial and banking companies with a presence in India need prior approval of the sectoral regulator. IDRs are denominated in Indian rupees only, and the issue proceeds are repatriated outside India immediately by the issuing company. A foreign portfolio investor, non-resident Indian or overseas citizen may buy, hold or sell IDRs (NRIs from their non-resident accounts). There is an overall cap on capital raised through IDRs by eligible foreign companies, monitored by the securities regulator. IDRs cannot be redeemed into underlying shares before one year; limited two-way fungibility allows listed Indian companies and Indian mutual funds to hold or sell the underlying shares and other residents to hold them for sale within 30 days of conversion. The courseware summarises that IDRs are rupee-denominated receipts issued to Indian investors by an overseas entity, convertible into a pre-specified number of shares of that entity.

External commercial borrowings (courseware, concept only): external commercial borrowings (ECB) are commercial loans raised by eligible resident entities from recognised non-resident lenders and must conform to parameters such as minimum maturity, permitted and non-permitted end-uses and maximum all-in-cost ceiling. The framework distinguishes ECB in foreign currency (loans including bank loans, floating or fixed rate notes, bonds and debentures other than fully and compulsorily convertible instruments, trade credits beyond three years, foreign currency convertible bonds, financial leases) and ECB in Indian rupees (loans, notes, bonds, preference shares other than fully convertible instruments, financial leases and plain vanilla rupee denominated bonds issued overseas). Eligible borrowers are entities eligible to receive FDI and certain other entities; recognised lenders are residents of countries that are compliant with international financial action and securities regulator standards, including multilateral financial institutions, with limits on individuals as lenders. Each ECB is subject to a minimum average maturity period that depends on the category and the use (call and put options not exercisable before it), an all-in-cost ceiling over a benchmark, a negative list of end-uses (such as real estate activities, investment in the capital market and equity, and in general working capital and repayment of rupee loans except in specified categories), a limit per financial year under the automatic route and, for foreign currency ECB, a leverage ratio. Domestic banks and financial institutions may not guarantee ECB repayment or invest in foreign currency convertible bonds. The particular tenors, spreads, limits and ratios are not taught.

Exchange rate, hedging and change of currency of ECB (courseware): in foreign currency ECB the exchange risk is borne by the Indian borrower; the borrower must follow hedging guidelines of the concerned regulator and have a board-approved risk management policy; infrastructure space companies must hedge a prescribed share of exposure where the average maturity is shorter than a stated period. The hedge must cover principal and coupon, start from the time the liability is created in the books, have a minimum tenor with periodic rollover so no unhedged period exists, and the designated authorised dealer bank verifies compliance and reports. A natural hedge counts only to the extent that projected cash flows in the matching currency (net of other outflows) offset the exposure within the same accounting year; arrangements where revenues are only indexed to foreign currency are not a natural hedge. For rupee ECB the overseas investor bears the exchange risk and may hedge through permitted derivatives with authorised dealers or branches of foreign banks with Indian presence on a back to back basis. Change of currency from one foreign currency to another is permitted for foreign currency ECB, as well as conversion into rupee (at the exchange rate prevailing on the date of the agreement or lower if consented to by the lender); change from rupee to a foreign currency is not permitted. Prepayment charge or penal interest is outside the all-in-cost ceiling but not above a limit.

Trade credits (courseware, concept only): trade credit (TC) is credit extended by an overseas supplier, bank, financial institution or other permitted lender for imports of capital or non-capital goods permitted under the Foreign Trade Policy; forms are suppliers credit (from the supplier of goods located outside India) and buyers credit (from banks, financial institutions, foreign equity holders or financial institutions in international financial services centres). The eligible borrower is a resident importer. Trade credit can be raised in a freely convertible foreign currency or in Indian rupees; the framework prescribes an amount limit under the automatic route per import transaction (higher for certain sectors), a maximum period (up to three years for capital goods; for non-capital goods the lesser of one year or the operating cycle, with exceptions for shipyards and shipbuilders) and an all-in-cost ceiling over a benchmark; the hedging, change of currency and exchange rate provisions are similar to ECB. Domestic banks cannot guarantee repayment of trade credits. The particular limits, periods and spreads are not taught.

Rupee denominated bonds issued overseas by banks (courseware, concept only): the central bank permitted banks to issue rupee denominated bonds overseas for perpetual debt instruments qualifying as Additional Tier 1 capital under Basel III, debt capital instruments qualifying as Tier 2 capital, and financing of infrastructure and affordable housing, subject to prudential norms and FEMA. The eligible amount for issue of perpetual debt instruments in foreign currency is, as at 31 March of the previous financial year, the higher of 1.5 per cent of risk weighted assets and the total Additional Tier 1 capital. Not more than 49 per cent of the eligible amount can be issued in foreign currency and or rupee denominated bonds overseas; rupee denominated bonds issued have to be excluded from the limit for investments by foreign portfolio investors in corporate bonds. The percentages are the courseware figures as at 2016 and are not taught.

Summary of risk bearing and unit overview (courseware): the unit gives an overview of funding options from overseas markets through debt and equity instruments and the risk accruing to the Indian entity as well as the overseas investor or lender. Summary points: GDRs and ADRs are tradable receipts in foreign currency in overseas markets convertible into a specified number of equity shares of the Indian company; IDRs are rupee denominated receipts issued by an overseas entity to Indian investors, convertible into a pre-specified number of shares of that entity; ECBs are loans raised in foreign currency or rupees by Indian entities and the exchange risk is borne by the borrowing company in India (for foreign currency ECB); ECB raised in rupees cannot be converted into foreign currency; domestic banks are prohibited from guaranteeing repayment of ECB; trade credits come with a maximum tenor of one year for non-capital imports and three years for capital imports (as at the courseware date).

payload.title: Foreign investment: FDI, FPI and fully diluted basis
payload.core_explanation_md:
Foreign investment in India is regulated under **FEMA, 1999** and its regulations on **transfer or issue of securities to persons resident outside India**.

| Term | Meaning (courseware) |
| --- | --- |
| **FDI** | Investment in capital instruments by a non-resident in an **unlisted** company, or in **10 per cent or more** of the post-issue paid-up equity of a **listed** company, on a **fully diluted** basis |
| **FPI** | Investment in a listed company **below 10 per cent** on a fully diluted basis |
| **Foreign portfolio investor** | A person **registered** under the securities regulator **FPI regulations** |
| **Foreign investment** | Any non-resident investment **on a repatriable basis** in capital instruments of an Indian company or an LLP |

**Fully diluted basis** = the **total shares that would exist if all sources of conversion were exercised**. If an FDI later **falls below 10 per cent**, it **continues to be treated as FDI**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The threshold is a classification test: it separates strategic holdings from portfolio holdings.

self_check.prompt_text: What does fully diluted basis mean?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Counting all shares that would be outstanding if every possible conversion were exercised.

payload.title: Sectors closed to foreign investment (concept)
payload.core_explanation_md:
Foreign investment is **prohibited** in listed sectors, including **lottery, gambling and betting**, **chit funds** (except non-repatriation investment by NRIs and OCIs), **nidhi companies**, **trading in transferable development rights**, **real estate business and farmhouse construction**, **tobacco product manufacturing**, and activities **reserved for the state** (such as **atomic energy and railway operations**). **Foreign technology collaboration** for lottery, gambling and betting is also prohibited.

Investors who are **citizens or entities of certain neighbouring countries** need **prior government approval**.

The list is as stated at the courseware date; **check the current list** before relying on it.

payload.title: Global Depository Receipts and ADRs
payload.core_explanation_md:
A **GDR** is a **negotiable receipt** issued by an **overseas depository** and traded in **overseas markets**. It entitles the holder to convert into a **specified number of equity shares** of an Indian company.

- The **underlying shares** are issued by the Indian company and held by an **Indian custodian** for the depository.
- GDRs are in **foreign currency**; the **overseas investor bears the exchange risk**.
- The number of shares per GDR is fixed under **pricing norms**.
- On issue, **equity increases** but the **debt-equity ratio is not adversely affected**.
- **Dividend** is paid in **rupees to the depository**; the depository **votes** the shares on behalf of the holders.
- **Limited two-way fungibility:** a registered broker may buy shares for conversion into receipts, and receipts that were redeemed may be **reissued** up to the originally approved total.
- **ADRs** are GDR-type receipts **traded in the United States**, with disclosure under US norms.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The company raises equity capital in foreign currency while investors hold a tradable receipt.

self_check.prompt_text: Who bears the exchange risk on a GDR?

payload.title: Indian Depository Receipts
payload.core_explanation_md:
An **IDR** is issued in **India** by a company **incorporated outside India**, through a **domestic depository**.

- **Denominated in rupees only**; **proceeds are repatriated** abroad by the issuer at once.
- Buyers: **residents**, and also FPIs, NRIs and OCIs (NRIs from non-resident accounts).
- **Financial and banking companies** with a presence in India need the **sectoral regulator approval**.
- An **overall cap** applies to IDR capital raised and is monitored by the securities regulator.
- **Redemption** into underlying shares is **not allowed for one year**; **limited two-way fungibility** applies (listed Indian companies and Indian mutual funds may hold or sell the shares; other residents must sell within 30 days of conversion).

**In short:** a rupee receipt issued to Indian investors by a foreign entity, convertible into a **pre-specified number of that entity shares**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: An IDR is the mirror image of a GDR: foreign company, Indian investors, rupee instrument.

self_check.prompt_text: In which currency are IDRs denominated?

payload.title: External commercial borrowings: structure
payload.core_explanation_md:
**ECB** = commercial loans raised by **eligible resident entities** from **recognised non-resident lenders**, subject to **minimum maturity, permitted end-uses and an all-in-cost ceiling**.

| | ECB in foreign currency | ECB in rupees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Instruments** | Bank loans, floating or fixed rate notes, bonds and debentures (not fully or compulsorily convertible), trade credits beyond three years, **FCCBs**, financial leases | Loans, notes, bonds, preference shares (not fully convertible), financial leases, **plain vanilla rupee bonds issued overseas** |
| **Exchange risk** | **Indian borrower** | **Overseas investor** |

**Common design features:** **eligible borrowers**, **recognised lenders**, **minimum average maturity** (call and put options not before it), **all-in-cost ceiling over a benchmark**, **negative end-use list** (for example **real estate**, **capital market investment**, **equity**, and generally **working capital** and **repayment of rupee loans** except in specified categories), a **per-year limit** under the automatic route and a **leverage ratio** for foreign currency ECB.

**Domestic banks and financial institutions may not guarantee ECB** or invest in FCCBs. Specific numbers are **not taught**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The rules aim to keep foreign borrowing long-dated, productive and not excessively costly.

self_check.prompt_text: Who bears the exchange risk in a foreign currency ECB?

payload.title: Hedging and change of currency for ECB
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Foreign currency ECB:** the borrower must follow **hedging guidelines** and keep a **board-approved risk management policy**; certain **infrastructure companies** must hedge a **prescribed share** when average maturity is short.

**Hedge design:**

- Cover **both principal and coupon**.
- Start when the **liability is created in the books**.
- **Minimum tenor with periodic rollover**, so there is **never an unhedged period**.
- The **authorised dealer bank verifies** compliance and **reports**.
- **Natural hedge** counts only to the extent that **projected cash flows in the matching currency** (net of other outflows) offset the exposure within the same accounting year; **revenue merely indexed** to foreign currency is **not** a natural hedge.

**Rupee ECB:** the **overseas investor bears the risk** and may hedge through **permitted derivatives**, including **back to back** arrangements with foreign bank branches.

**Change of currency:** foreign currency to **another foreign currency** or to **rupees** is allowed (at the rate on the agreement date or lower if the lender agrees); **rupee to foreign currency is not allowed**. **Prepayment charges or penal interest** are **outside** the all-in-cost ceiling but capped.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A hedge that ends before the loan does leaves a period of open exposure.

self_check.prompt_text: Is a revenue stream merely indexed to a foreign currency a natural hedge?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No; only offsetting projected cash flows in the matching currency count.

payload.title: Trade credits
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Trade credit (TC)** is credit from an **overseas supplier, bank, financial institution** or other permitted lender for **imports of capital or non-capital goods** allowed under the **Foreign Trade Policy**.

| Form | Source |
| --- | --- |
| **Suppliers credit** | The **supplier of goods located outside India** |
| **Buyers credit** | **Banks, financial institutions, foreign equity holders**, or institutions in **IFSCs** |

- The **borrower** is a **resident importer**.
- TC may be in a **freely convertible foreign currency** or in **rupees**.
- The framework sets an **amount limit per import transaction**, a **maximum period** (longer for capital goods than for non-capital goods) and an **all-in-cost ceiling over a benchmark**; **hedging, change of currency and exchange rate** rules resemble ECB.
- **Domestic banks cannot guarantee** repayment of trade credits.

Limits, periods and spreads are **not taught**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Trade credit finances a specific import, unlike a general-purpose ECB.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Trade credit for an import arranged by a bank or financial institution outside India (or in an IFSC) rather than by the supplier.

payload.title: Rupee denominated bonds of banks and unit summary
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Rupee denominated bonds** may be issued overseas by banks for:

- **Perpetual debt instruments** qualifying as **Additional Tier 1** capital.
- **Debt capital instruments** qualifying as **Tier 2** capital.
- Financing of **infrastructure and affordable housing**.

The **eligible amount** for perpetual debt is, at the previous 31 March, the **higher of** a stated percentage of **risk weighted assets** and the **total Additional Tier 1 capital**; **rupee bonds issued overseas are excluded** from the limit on **FPI investment in corporate bonds**. (Courseware percentages are **not taught**.)

**Risk bearing across the instruments:**

| Instrument | Currency | Who bears exchange risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **GDR / ADR** | Foreign currency | **Overseas investor** |
| **IDR** | Rupees | **Overseas issuer** (receives and repatriates rupees) |
| **Foreign currency ECB** | Foreign currency | **Indian borrower** |
| **Rupee ECB / rupee bonds abroad** | Rupees | **Overseas investor** |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The currency of denomination largely decides who carries the exchange risk.

payload.title: Hedge ratio and unhedged exposure
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Hedge ratio = hedged amount / total exposure.**

**Unhedged exposure = total exposure - hedged amount.**

**Rupee cost of repayment = foreign currency amount x exchange rate at repayment.**

**Exchange loss (or gain) = foreign currency amount x (repayment rate - rate at drawdown).**

Example: **USD 10 million** drawn at **Rs 82** and repaid at **Rs 85** with **no hedge**: loss **10 x 3 = Rs 30 million**. A **70 per cent hedge** leaves **USD 3 million** unhedged: loss **Rs 9 million**.

assumptions: The hedge locks the rate for the hedged part
common_errors: Applying the rate change to the hedged part
Using the wrong direction of change

payload.expanded_explanation_md: A weaker rupee raises the rupee cost of repaying foreign currency debt.

self_check.prompt_text: Who gains if the rupee weakens after a foreign currency ECB is drawn?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No one on the borrowing side: the borrower pays more rupees; only a hedged borrower is protected.

items.title: Foreign investment: FDI, FPI and fully diluted basis
items.core_explanation_md:
Foreign investment in India is regulated under **FEMA, 1999** and its regulations on **transfer or issue of securities to persons resident outside India**.

| Term | Meaning (courseware) |
| --- | --- |
| **FDI** | Investment in capital instruments by a non-resident in an **unlisted** company, or in **10 per cent or more** of the post-issue paid-up equity of a **listed** company, on a **fully diluted** basis |
| **FPI** | Investment in a listed company **below 10 per cent** on a fully diluted basis |
| **Foreign portfolio investor** | A person **registered** under the securities regulator **FPI regulations** |
| **Foreign investment** | Any non-resident investment **on a repatriable basis** in capital instruments of an Indian company or an LLP |

**Fully diluted basis** = the **total shares that would exist if all sources of conversion were exercised**. If an FDI later **falls below 10 per cent**, it **continues to be treated as FDI**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The threshold is a classification test: it separates strategic holdings from portfolio holdings.

self_check.prompt_text: What does fully diluted basis mean?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Counting all shares that would be outstanding if every possible conversion were exercised.

items.title: Sectors closed to foreign investment (concept)
items.core_explanation_md:
Foreign investment is **prohibited** in listed sectors, including **lottery, gambling and betting**, **chit funds** (except non-repatriation investment by NRIs and OCIs), **nidhi companies**, **trading in transferable development rights**, **real estate business and farmhouse construction**, **tobacco product manufacturing**, and activities **reserved for the state** (such as **atomic energy and railway operations**). **Foreign technology collaboration** for lottery, gambling and betting is also prohibited.

Investors who are **citizens or entities of certain neighbouring countries** need **prior government approval**.

The list is as stated at the courseware date; **check the current list** before relying on it.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Prohibitions apply whatever the route or the size of the stake.

items.title: Global Depository Receipts and ADRs
items.core_explanation_md:
A **GDR** is a **negotiable receipt** issued by an **overseas depository** and traded in **overseas markets**. It entitles the holder to convert into a **specified number of equity shares** of an Indian company.

- The **underlying shares** are issued by the Indian company and held by an **Indian custodian** for the depository.
- GDRs are in **foreign currency**; the **overseas investor bears the exchange risk**.
- The number of shares per GDR is fixed under **pricing norms**.
- On issue, **equity increases** but the **debt-equity ratio is not adversely affected**.
- **Dividend** is paid in **rupees to the depository**; the depository **votes** the shares on behalf of the holders.
- **Limited two-way fungibility:** a registered broker may buy shares for conversion into receipts, and receipts that were redeemed may be **reissued** up to the originally approved total.
- **ADRs** are GDR-type receipts **traded in the United States**, with disclosure under US norms.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The company raises equity capital in foreign currency while investors hold a tradable receipt.

items.title: Indian Depository Receipts
items.core_explanation_md:
An **IDR** is issued in **India** by a company **incorporated outside India**, through a **domestic depository**.

- **Denominated in rupees only**; **proceeds are repatriated** abroad by the issuer at once.
- Buyers: **residents**, and also FPIs, NRIs and OCIs (NRIs from non-resident accounts).
- **Financial and banking companies** with a presence in India need the **sectoral regulator approval**.
- An **overall cap** applies to IDR capital raised and is monitored by the securities regulator.
- **Redemption** into underlying shares is **not allowed for one year**; **limited two-way fungibility** applies (listed Indian companies and Indian mutual funds may hold or sell the shares; other residents must sell within 30 days of conversion).

**In short:** a rupee receipt issued to Indian investors by a foreign entity, convertible into a **pre-specified number of that entity shares**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: An IDR is the mirror image of a GDR: foreign company, Indian investors, rupee instrument.

items.title: External commercial borrowings: structure
items.core_explanation_md:
**ECB** = commercial loans raised by **eligible resident entities** from **recognised non-resident lenders**, subject to **minimum maturity, permitted end-uses and an all-in-cost ceiling**.

| | ECB in foreign currency | ECB in rupees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Instruments** | Bank loans, floating or fixed rate notes, bonds and debentures (not fully or compulsorily convertible), trade credits beyond three years, **FCCBs**, financial leases | Loans, notes, bonds, preference shares (not fully convertible), financial leases, **plain vanilla rupee bonds issued overseas** |
| **Exchange risk** | **Indian borrower** | **Overseas investor** |

**Common design features:** **eligible borrowers**, **recognised lenders**, **minimum average maturity** (call and put options not before it), **all-in-cost ceiling over a benchmark**, **negative end-use list** (for example **real estate**, **capital market investment**, **equity**, and generally **working capital** and **repayment of rupee loans** except in specified categories), a **per-year limit** under the automatic route and a **leverage ratio** for foreign currency ECB.

**Domestic banks and financial institutions may not guarantee ECB** or invest in FCCBs. Specific numbers are **not taught**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The rules aim to keep foreign borrowing long-dated, productive and not excessively costly.

items.title: Hedging and change of currency for ECB
items.core_explanation_md:
**Foreign currency ECB:** the borrower must follow **hedging guidelines** and keep a **board-approved risk management policy**; certain **infrastructure companies** must hedge a **prescribed share** when average maturity is short.

**Hedge design:**

- Cover **both principal and coupon**.
- Start when the **liability is created in the books**.
- **Minimum tenor with periodic rollover**, so there is **never an unhedged period**.
- The **authorised dealer bank verifies** compliance and **reports**.
- **Natural hedge** counts only to the extent that **projected cash flows in the matching currency** (net of other outflows) offset the exposure within the same accounting year; **revenue merely indexed** to foreign currency is **not** a natural hedge.

**Rupee ECB:** the **overseas investor bears the risk** and may hedge through **permitted derivatives**, including **back to back** arrangements with foreign bank branches.

**Change of currency:** foreign currency to **another foreign currency** or to **rupees** is allowed (at the rate on the agreement date or lower if the lender agrees); **rupee to foreign currency is not allowed**. **Prepayment charges or penal interest** are **outside** the all-in-cost ceiling but capped.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A hedge that ends before the loan does leaves a period of open exposure.

self_check.prompt_text: Is a revenue stream merely indexed to a foreign currency a natural hedge?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No; only offsetting projected cash flows in the matching currency count.

items.title: Trade credits
items.core_explanation_md:
**Trade credit (TC)** is credit from an **overseas supplier, bank, financial institution** or other permitted lender for **imports of capital or non-capital goods** allowed under the **Foreign Trade Policy**.

| Form | Source |
| --- | --- |
| **Suppliers credit** | The **supplier of goods located outside India** |
| **Buyers credit** | **Banks, financial institutions, foreign equity holders**, or institutions in **IFSCs** |

- The **borrower** is a **resident importer**.
- TC may be in a **freely convertible foreign currency** or in **rupees**.
- The framework sets an **amount limit per import transaction**, a **maximum period** (longer for capital goods than for non-capital goods) and an **all-in-cost ceiling over a benchmark**; **hedging, change of currency and exchange rate** rules resemble ECB.
- **Domestic banks cannot guarantee** repayment of trade credits.

Limits, periods and spreads are **not taught**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Trade credit finances a specific import, unlike a general-purpose ECB.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Trade credit for an import arranged by a bank or financial institution outside India (or in an IFSC) rather than by the supplier.

items.title: Rupee denominated bonds of banks and unit summary
items.core_explanation_md:
**Rupee denominated bonds** may be issued overseas by banks for:

- **Perpetual debt instruments** qualifying as **Additional Tier 1** capital.
- **Debt capital instruments** qualifying as **Tier 2** capital.
- Financing of **infrastructure and affordable housing**.

The **eligible amount** for perpetual debt is, at the previous 31 March, the **higher of** a stated percentage of **risk weighted assets** and the **total Additional Tier 1 capital**; **rupee bonds issued overseas are excluded** from the limit on **FPI investment in corporate bonds**. (Courseware percentages are **not taught**.)

**Risk bearing across the instruments:**

| Instrument | Currency | Who bears exchange risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **GDR / ADR** | Foreign currency | **Overseas investor** |
| **IDR** | Rupees | **Overseas issuer** (receives and repatriates rupees) |
| **Foreign currency ECB** | Foreign currency | **Indian borrower** |
| **Rupee ECB / rupee bonds abroad** | Rupees | **Overseas investor** |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The currency of denomination largely decides who carries the exchange risk.

items.title: Hedge ratio and unhedged exposure
items.core_explanation_md:
**Hedge ratio = hedged amount / total exposure.**

**Unhedged exposure = total exposure - hedged amount.**

**Rupee cost of repayment = foreign currency amount x exchange rate at repayment.**

**Exchange loss (or gain) = foreign currency amount x (repayment rate - rate at drawdown).**

Example: **USD 10 million** drawn at **Rs 82** and repaid at **Rs 85** with **no hedge**: loss **10 x 3 = Rs 30 million**. A **70 per cent hedge** leaves **USD 3 million** unhedged: loss **Rs 9 million**.
